lead: Tape-in and clip-in hair extensions are add-on wefts or strands of human or synthetic hair that attach to natural hair, using adhesive tape or small clips, to add length, volume or thickness. People use them to get a fuller head of hair or a longer style right away, including to disguise thinning at the crown or hairline.[1]

Wikipedia lists tape-in and clip-in or clip-on among the main attachment methods for hair extensions, alongside micro or nano rings, fusion, weaving and wigs.[1] Clip-ins are put in and taken out by the wearer, whereas tape-ins are bonded to the hair for a period of weeks.[1] Human hair is the more durable option, while synthetic fibres such as Kanekalon are cheaper but less durable and can look stiffer.[1]

The main documented concern is tension. Traction alopecia, hair loss from ongoing pulling, is described as a result of tight styles and of extensions or weaves attached to tightly braided hair.[2] Glue-based methods have also been linked to dermatitis and headaches.[1]

angle.text: Extensions add visible hair where there is little, so the style looks longer or thicker while they are worn. Clip-ins can be put in for a day and taken out; tape-ins stay in for weeks.

infobox: Human hair or synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon[1]
Clip-ins are removable; some other methods last about eight weeks[1]

paras: Extensions come as wefts or single strands. Human hair is the premium material and most commonly comes from India, China and Vietnam; tangle-free versions have the cuticle chemically removed and a coating added for shine.[1] Synthetic fibres are cheaper and less durable, and heat styling tools generally are not used on them, although heat-resistant fibres exist.[1]

Methods of integration listed include track-and-sew, bonding glue, invisible-part techniques, thread sewing, tape-in and clip-in or clip-on.[1] A sew-in invisible-part installation is reported to take about an hour and last roughly eight weeks.[1]
Wigs were a fashion trend by the late 17th century. Hair weaves appeared in the 1950s, initially among celebrities, and became widespread in the 1970s.[1]

Extensions are used to change hair length or add density without waiting for growth, and in grooming discussions they appear as a non-surgical way to add apparent hair volume. Clip-ins suit occasions where the wearer wants to put them in and remove them the same day.

No studies found on tape-in or clip-in extensions for appearance. Dermatology descriptions of traction alopecia name tight styles, weaves and extensions attached to tightly braided hair as causes, with hairline recession at the temples and sides as the typical pattern.[2]

Wikipedia reports that prolonged wear or tight attachment can cause traction alopecia, which may become permanent, and can cause breakage and split ends.[1][2] Glue-based methods have been linked to headaches, bald spots and dermatitis, and bonding wefts directly to the scalp can irritate it.[1] In traction alopecia, treatment focuses on removing the tension, and surgery is reserved for severe scarring cases.[2]

timeline.event: Hair weaves appear, mainly among celebrities.[1]

name: Hair tape-in / clip-in extensions

card.summary: Add-on hair wefts that attach by adhesive tape or clips for instant volume and length; the main documented risk is tension and adhesive damage to natural hair.
card.note: Prolonged tension or adhesive use is linked to traction alopecia and dermatitis.

quick.overview:
Tape-in and clip-in extensions are strands or wefts of human or synthetic hair that are attached to a person's own hair to add length or thickness. Clip-ins are fastened and removed by the wearer with small clips, while tape-ins are bonded to the natural hair with adhesive strips.

In appearance communities they are discussed as a way to add visible volume without a procedure, mostly by people with thin or short hair. No clinical trials were found that test their appearance benefit.
quick.mechanism: Hair wefts are attached to the natural hair (not the scalp) by clips or adhesive tape, adding visible density and length. They do not affect the underlying hair or follicles.
quick.risks: Dermatology references describe traction alopecia (hair loss at the hairline or around the ears) from prolonged tension, and adhesives can cause dermatitis or headaches. Wikipedia notes patch testing is advised before using bonding products.
